cards.a: A constructed language built around a small core vocabulary and a simple, regular grammar. Instead of naming things precisely, it names broad concepts and leaves you to combine and narrow them with context — a deliberate constraint that shapes how you think about what you're saying, not just how you say it.

cards.q: What does the name "toki pona" mean?
cards.a: Literally good language or simple language — toki means language/speech/to talk, and pona means good/simple. The name is also a small demonstration: it's built entirely from words the language itself teaches you in this course.

cards.q: Who created Toki Pona, and when?
cards.a: The Canadian linguist and translator Sonja Lang, who published its core vocabulary online in 2001 and spent the following thirteen years refining it with the community that grew up around it — work that culminated in the 2014 book Toki Pona: The Language of Good. The whole project began as a personal philosophical question she set out to answer: how few concepts can a language get away with while staying genuinely usable for daily life?

cards.q: Why does Toki Pona use so few words?
cards.a: Its core vocabulary is about 120 words — tiny next to a natural language's tens of thousands. The deliberate constraint encourages speakers to break ideas into broad, relevant qualities and rely on context instead of reaching for a separate word for every distinction.

cards.q: If the vocabulary is so small, how do you say specific things?
cards.a: By combining words. There's no word for "car," but tomo tawa — "moving container/building" — gets there, and context narrows it further. The trade is precision for effort: you say less exactly, but you say it fast, and the listener fills in the rest from context, the same way you'd understand "the vehicle" from context without needing "vehicle" to specify make and model.

cards.q: Is Toki Pona meant to replace other languages?
cards.a: No. People generally learn it as an additional language, for the community around it, as a thinking exercise, for art, or simply for the fun of a genuinely different design. It is not tied to a country and was not designed to become a universal language.

cards.q: Does Toki Pona have its own writing system?
cards.a: The language itself is usually written with the Latin alphabet, exactly as it's taught here. A separate optional script, sitelen pona, represents each word as a small pictogram instead of letters — popular in the community for art and signage, but not needed to read, speak, or study the language.

cards.q: Build a Toki Pona phrase for "car" from "tomo" (building/container) and "tawa" (moving).
cards.a: tomo tawa — literally "moving building/container."

cards.q: How many vowels does Toki Pona have, and how are they pronounced?
cards.a: Five: a e i o u, pronounced roughly as in Spanish or Italian — a as in "father," e as in "bed," i as in "machine," o as in "more," u as in "food." These are five vowel categories rather than five rigid accent-free sounds, so speakers' exact pronunciation can vary. Standard spelling has no silent letters.

cards.q: How many consonants does Toki Pona have?
cards.a: Nine: j k l m n p s t w. j is pronounced like English "y" (as in "yes"), and w like English "w." The rest sound close to their English values. Letters like b, c, d, f, g, h, q, r, v, x, y, and z do not appear in standard Toki Pona spelling.

cards.q: What is the basic shape of a Toki Pona syllable?
cards.a: The first syllable has an optional consonant, then a vowel, then an optional n: (C)V(n). Every later syllable must begin with a consonant: CV(n). a, pi, tan, and mun are all complete, valid syllables on their own; a word is just one or more valid syllables joined together, like to-ki or mu-si.

cards.q: Which syllable is stressed in a Toki Pona word?
cards.a: Always the first one. PO-na, not po-NA; TO-ki, not to-KI. The rule never has exceptions, which makes an unfamiliar word easy to pronounce correctly on sight.

cards.q: Are consonant clusters allowed within a word?
cards.a: Two consonants can sit side by side across a syllable boundary when the first is a final n, as in an-pa, ten-po, and lin-ja. Within a syllable, there is at most one opening consonant and the only possible final consonant is n. The sequences nn and nm are avoided, as are the syllables ji, ti, wo, and wu. Before p, a written n may sound like m, but it is still spelled n.

cards.q: How are foreign names adapted into Toki Pona's sounds?
cards.a: By adapting their pronunciation, not simply their spelling, to Toki Pona's sounds and valid syllables. Unavailable sounds are approximated, consonant clusters are reshaped, and every noninitial syllable receives an opening consonant. "Canada" is commonly adapted as Kanata; other names may have several reasonable forms because speakers prioritize recognizability differently. An adaptation must still avoid ji, ti, wo, wu, nn, and nm.

cards.q: Why is "Kalauto" not a valid Toki Pona name?
cards.a: It divides as ka-la-u-to, leaving the noninitial syllable u without an opening consonant. Only a word's first syllable may begin with a vowel, so a speaker would need to choose a different adaptation.

cards.q: Which spelling follows Toki Pona phonotactics: "tenpo" or "timo"?
cards.a: tenpo. It divides into the valid syllables ten-po; the adjacent np lies across that boundary. timo begins with the forbidden syllable ti.

cards.q: What is the basic word order in a Toki Pona sentence?
cards.a: Subject, then predicate, then object — the same SVO order English uses. jan li moku e kili breaks down as "person" + [predicate marker] "eats" + [object marker] "fruit": the person eats fruit.

It marks the start of the predicate — everything from li onward is what the subject does or is. jan li pona is "the person is good"; soweli li moku is "the animal eats." Without li, a listener can't tell where the subject ends and the action begins.

cards.q: When does a sentence NOT need "li"?
cards.a: When the subject is exactly mi (I/we) or sina (you) on its own, with nothing else describing it. mi moku is "I eat," not mi li moku. Add anything to the subject — a second noun, a modifier — and li comes back: mi mute li moku, "we (many) eat."

It marks the direct object, the thing the action is done to. In mi moku e kili, e shows that kili (fruit) is what gets eaten, not a second subject. Without e, a string of nouns after the verb would just pile up with no way to tell object from description.

cards.q: How does Toki Pona show tense — past, present, or future?
cards.a: It mostly doesn't grammatically; the same sentence can describe past, present, or future action, and context (or an added time word like tenpo pini, "past time") carries the difference when it matters. Verbs never conjugate.

cards.q: How does Toki Pona show whether a noun is singular or plural?
cards.a: It generally doesn't mark this either — soweli can mean "animal" or "animals" depending on context. Where the count genuinely matters, a number or a word like mute ("many") is added instead of an ending.

cards.q: How can the same word be a noun, a verb, and a describing word?
cards.a: Many Toki Pona content words are flexible: syntax and context let the same word fill noun-like, predicate, or modifier roles. moku can be "food," "eat," or "edible/food-related" depending on its place in a phrase. This flexibility does not apply identically to every word; particles such as li and e, prepositions, and preverbs have grammatical jobs of their own.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "I eat fruit."
cards.a: mi moku e kili. The subject is exactly mi, so it does not take li; e marks kili as the object.

cards.q: Correct "jan li pona moku e kili" so it means "The person is good and eats fruit."
cards.a: jan li pona li moku e kili. Repeat li to introduce each predicate belonging to the same subject.

cards.q: Where does a modifier go relative to the word it describes?
cards.a: Directly after it. tomo pona is "good house" (house + good); modifiers always follow, never precede, the word they change — the opposite order from English adjectives.

cards.q: How do multiple modifiers stack on one noun?
cards.a: They build from left to right. Each new modifier describes the entire phrase formed before it: jan pona mi groups as (jan pona) mi, "my good person/friend." It does not group as jan (pona mi), "a person of my goodness," unless pi explicitly starts that new modifier group.

cards.q: What problem does the particle "pi" solve?
cards.a: By default, a phrase builds from left to right. pi starts a new modifier group so the words after it are understood together before they modify the phrase before pi. It is used when the intended grouping differs from the default, and it normally introduces at least two content words rather than a single modifier.

cards.q: How does "pi" change the meaning of a phrase?
cards.a: Compare jan lawa mute, which groups as (jan lawa) mute and means "many leaders," with jan lawa pi ma tomo, where pi groups ma tomo, "city," before it modifies jan lawa, "leader." pi starts a fresh modifier group; it is not a general-purpose translation of English "of."

cards.q: How do you negate a word with "ala"?
cards.a: Place ala right after it, the same slot any other modifier fills. jan pona is "a good person"; jan pona ala is "a person who is not good." mi wile ala is "I don't want to" — ala negates whatever it directly follows, not the whole sentence.

cards.q: Does a modifier ever come before the word it describes?
cards.a: No, that ordering is fixed. The one common exception in how modifiers are talked about is a proper name used as a modifier of jan or ma ("jan Sonja," "ma Kanata") — it still follows the pattern, since the name modifies the general word before it, just like any other description.

cards.q: How does "jan toki pona" group without "pi"?
cards.a: As (jan toki) pona: a good speaker. The final modifier pona describes the whole phrase jan toki.

cards.q: How do you say "person of good speech" using "pi"?
cards.a: jan pi toki pona. The pi makes toki pona, "good speech/language," a group that modifies jan.

It joins two or more subjects into one. jan en soweli li moku is "the person and the animal eat" — without en, a second noun placed next to the first would just look like a modifier of it, not a separate thing doing the action too.

cards.q: Can "en" join objects, or only subjects?
cards.a: Only subjects. Toki Pona has no equivalent particle for joining two objects after e; instead, the object marker e is repeated for each one. mi moku e kili e telo is "I eat/drink fruit and water" — each e introduces its own object.

It marks a leading clause as context, condition, or setting for the sentence that follows — roughly "given this," "when this," or "if this." tenpo suno la mi moku is "in the daytime, I eat" (or "when it's day, I eat").

cards.q: Where does a "la" clause sit, and how is it written?
cards.a: The context comes before la, and the main sentence follows it: [context] la [main sentence]. A writer may add a comma after la for readability, but punctuation is optional rather than part of the grammar. sina wile la mi ken pana and sina wile la, mi ken pana both mean "if you want, I can give (it)."

cards.q: What does "anu" mean, and where is it used?
cards.a: "Or." sina wile e telo anu kili? is "do you want water or fruit?" — it links two alternatives the same way en links two things that are both true.

Most often "but" or "however," opening a sentence that qualifies or contradicts the one before it: mi wile e ni. taso, mi ken ala. — "I want this. But I can't." As a modifier after a word it can also mean "only" or "alone," so jan taso is "only a/the person" or "a person alone."

cards.q: How do you give one subject more than one predicate?
cards.a: For a subject that takes li, repeat it before each predicate: ona li pona li moku means "they are good and eat." Many modern speakers extend this pattern after bare mi or sina, omitting the first li but using it for later predicates: mi pona li moku. In stricter pu style, those become separate sentences: mi pona. mi moku.

cards.q: How do you say "The animal is good and eats fruit"?
cards.a: soweli li pona li moku e kili. The repeated li gives the one subject, soweli, two predicates.

cards.q: What does "lon" mean as a preposition, and as a quality on its own?
cards.a: As a preposition, "at," "in," or "on": mi lon tomo, "I am at home." Standing alone as a quality after li, it means "real," "true," or "present": ni li lon, "this is real" or "this exists."

cards.q: What does "tawa" mean, both as a preposition and as a verb?
cards.a: As a preposition, "to" or "toward": mi tawa tomo, "I go to the house." As a verb on its own it's "to move" or "to go." It's also used to mean "for," from someone's point of view: ni li pona tawa mi, "this is good, to me" — "I think this is good."
"From" a place, or "because of/due to" a cause. mi tan ma Kanata is "I'm from Canada"; mi moku tan wile is "I eat because of hunger," using wile (want/need) as the reason.

cards.q: What does "kepeken" mean, as a preposition and as a verb?
cards.a: In core pu grammar, kepeken is the preposition "using" or "with" an instrument: mi pali kepeken ilo, "I work using a tool." Transitive kepeken e, as in mi kepeken e ilo for "I use the tool," appeared in early usage and is still used by some speakers, but pu teaches the prepositional pattern and most speakers prefer it today.

"Like," "same as," or "similar to," comparing two things: ona li sama mi, "they are like me" or "they are the same as me." As a modifier after a noun it can also mean "fellow" or "peer" — jan sama, someone on the same level.

cards.q: What does "poka" mean, and how does it express location?
cards.a: In core pu grammar, poka is not itself a preposition. It is a content word meaning "side," "nearby area," or "hip": in poki li lon poka mi, "the container is next to me," lon is the preposition and poka mi is its object phrase, "my side." Some non-pu or variant usage treats poka directly as "beside" or "with," but that is not the core pattern taught here.

cards.q: In "poki li lon poka mi," which word is the preposition?
cards.a: lon. The phrase poka mi, "my side," is the object of the preposition; poka is a content word here.

cards.q: How do you say "I work using a tool" without putting "e" after "kepeken"?
cards.a: mi pali kepeken ilo. Here kepeken is a preposition introducing the instrument ilo.

cards.q: What does "seme" do, and where does it go in a sentence?
cards.a: It's the question word for "what" or "which," and it sits exactly where the answer would go, rather than moving to the front the way English "what" does. sina wile e seme? is "you want [what]?" — "what do you want?" ni li seme? is "this is [what]?" — "what is this?"

cards.q: How do you ask a yes/no question in Toki Pona?
cards.a: By repeating the word being asked about with ala in between: sina moku ala moku?, literally "you eat not-eat?" — "do you eat?" The answer is usually just the word alone (moku for yes) or with ala (moku ala, or plain ala, for no).

cards.q: What does the particle "o" do in a command?
cards.a: It replaces li before the action, turning a statement into an instruction or suggestion aimed at the subject. sina o moku is "you should eat"; mi mute o tawa is "let's go" (we should go) — the subject can be "you," "we," or a third party being told what to do.

cards.q: How do you address someone directly using "o"?
cards.a: By placing o right after their name or description, as a stand-alone vocative — the "hey, [name]" of Toki Pona. jan Ana o, sina pona is "Jan Ana, you're good/kind," calling her attention before the sentence continues.

cards.q: What does adding "anu seme" to the end of a sentence do?
cards.a: It adds an open alternative, literally "or what/which?", and is also a common way to make a yes/no question. sina wile e ni, anu seme? asks whether you want this or not. Tone can make it sound tag-like, but it is not inherently the confirmation-seeking English "...right?"

cards.q: What does "ni" mean, and how is it used?
cards.a: "This" or "that," Toki Pona's one general demonstrative — it doesn't distinguish near from far the way English does. Alone it acts as a pronoun: ni li pona, "this is good." After a noun it acts as a modifier: tomo ni li suli, "this house is big."

cards.q: Correct "seme sina wile e?" so it asks "What do you want?"
cards.a: sina wile e seme? The question word stays in the same position that the answer would occupy.

cards.q: What are Toki Pona's core number words?
cards.a: Toki Pona commonly uses two number systems. In the simple system, ala is none/zero, wan is one, tu is two, mute is three or more/many, and ale/ali is all or an unbounded amount. In the extended exact system, ala is 0, wan is 1, tu is 2, luka is 5, mute is 20, and ale/ali is 100.

luka means "hand" or "arm," and one hand has five fingers. In the extended exact number system it therefore means exactly five. Context tells the uses apart: luka mi is "my hand," while kili luka can be "five fruits."

cards.q: What does "wan" mean, and how is it used beyond counting?
cards.a: "One." As a modifier it can also mean "a," "single," or "unified" — jan wan can be "one person" or "a united group of people," depending on context, the same doubling other quantity words show.

cards.q: What does "tu" mean, and how is it used beyond counting?
cards.a: "Two." As a modifier it can mean "a pair" or "divided into two" — describing something split or paired rather than only literally counting a pair of items.

cards.q: What can "mute" mean as a quantity or number?
cards.a: Many, much, several, or very. In the simple counting system it covers three or more without giving an exact total; in the extended exact system it has the value 20. Context and the counting convention tell those uses apart.

cards.q: Does Toki Pona have a word for zero?
cards.a: Yes — ala, the same word used to negate ("not"). Zero and "none" are the same idea in Toki Pona's small vocabulary: soweli ala is "no animals" or "zero animals."

cards.q: How do you talk about numbers larger than "two" precisely?
cards.a: Use the extended exact system and add the values together: tu wan is 3, tu tu is 4, luka tu is 7, and mute luka tu wan is 28. This additive system is useful for ordinary exact counts, although speakers may choose another convention when large numbers need to be communicated efficiently.

It marks a number as an ordinal — "-th" rather than a plain count. tomo nanpa tu is "house number two" or "the second house," turning tu from "two things" into "the second one." On its own, nanpa is simply the noun "number."

"All," "everything," or "every." jan ale li pona is "everyone is good." In the extended exact number system, it also has the value 100. ali is an alternate pronunciation and spelling that some speakers use to make it easier to distinguish from ala.
"Seven people eat." In the extended exact system, luka tu adds 5 and 2.

Person, human being, or somebody. It's also the word placed before a personal name: jan Ana is "the person named Ana," which is how Toki Pona introduces proper names into an otherwise tiny vocabulary.

"I," "me," "we," or "us." mi does not mark singular or plural; context can make either meaning clear. mi mute can emphasize "we" or "many of us," but it is not required for a plural meaning. A subject consisting of mi alone does not take li.
"You," singular or plural, with the same non-distinction as mi — sina can mean one listener or several. It's the other subject allowed to drop li.
"He," "she," "it," or "they" — Toki Pona's one third-person pronoun, covering every gender and number English splits apart. Which one is meant comes entirely from context.
Woman, girl, or something feminine — as a modifier it marks the feminine version of a more general word, the way jan meli narrows "person" to "woman."
Man, boy, or something masculine, the counterpart to meli: jan mije is "man," narrowing jan the same way.
Parent, ancestor, or caretaker — a broad family-and-origin word rather than specifically "mother" or "father." mama meli and mama mije narrow it to mother and father when the distinction matters.
Group, community, organization, or nation — any collection of people (or things) treated as one unit. kulupu mi can be "my group," "my team," or "my country," depending on scale.
To love, or love itself — deep affection or care, romantic or otherwise. mi olin e sina is "I love you"; as a noun it names the feeling directly.

cards.q: Translate: "mi mute li olin e kulupu ni."
cards.a: "We love this community." Because the subject is the phrase mi mute, not mi alone, it is followed by li.
Body — the whole physical form of a person or animal, as opposed to its mind or its individual parts. sijelo mi is "my body."
Head, literally — and by extension, to lead, control, or rule, and the mind or leader doing the controlling. lawa mi is "my head," while jan lawa is "the leader," the person who "heads" a group.
Leg or foot, and by extension the bottom or base of something — the part that carries the rest. noka mi is "my leg/foot"; noka tomo could describe a building's foundation.
Mouth, and by extension a doorway or opening something eats or speaks through. Most directly, it's the body part: uta mi, "my mouth."

Inside, interior, or stomach/belly — both the general idea of "the inside of something" and the specific body part where that's most obviously felt. insa tomo is "inside the house"; insa mi li ike is "my stomach feels bad."
Back (the body part) or behind — both the physical back and the position "behind" something. monsi mi is "my back"; monsi tomo is "behind the house."
Face, front, or wall — the front-facing surface of a person, a place, or a structure. sinpin mi is "my face"; sinpin tomo is "the front of the house" or "a wall."
Skin, peel, shell, or bark — and more generally, the outer layer or boundary of anything. selo mi is "my skin"; selo kili is a fruit's peel.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "My back is fine."
cards.a: monsi mi li pona.
Can, possible, or allowed — ability or permission, both handled by the same word. Before another predicate, it is a preverb: mi ken tawa is "I can go" or "I may go," with context sorting out which.
To hear or listen, and by extension the ear itself. mi kute e ona is "I hear/listen to them."
To see, look at, watch, examine, or read — and, as a noun, an eye or sight. mi lukin e ni is "I see/look at this." Before another predicate, lukin can be a preverb meaning "try to."
Fun, play, game, or art — anything entertaining, and the act of playing or having fun. ni li musi is "this is fun"; mi musi is "I'm playing/having fun."
To feel, an emotion, or the heart as the seat of feeling — both the physical sensation and the emotional one. pilin mi li pona is "I feel good" (literally "my feeling is good").
To know, knowledge, wisdom, or a skill. mi sona e ni is "I know this." Before another predicate, sona is a preverb meaning "know how to," so mi sona pali is "I know how to work/do things."
Language, speech, or to talk/speak/communicate — the same word that names the course itself. mi toki e ni is "I say this"; toki mi is "my language."

To want, need, wish, or should — desire and obligation share this one word. It often acts as a preverb: mi wile moku is "I want to eat"; sina wile pona can mean "you should be good/improve" or "you want to be good/improve."

A preverb comes before another predicate and changes how it applies. Common examples include wile (want/need to), ken (can), sona (know how to), kama (come to/become), and awen (continue to). In pu, lukin can mean "try to"; many modern speakers instead use alasa. open and pini are also used for "start to" and "stop doing." Unlike a modifier, a preverb appears before the predicate it affects.
"I can speak." ken is a preverb modifying toki.
"I know how to do/make this." sona is a preverb modifying pali.
Word or name — any unit of language, spoken or written, including what something or someone is called. nimi mi is "my name"; nimi ni li seme? is "what does this word mean?"
Image, picture, symbol, or writing — and, as a verb, to draw or write. mi sitelen e ni is "I draw/write this." It's also the root of sitelen pona, Toki Pona's optional pictogram script.

A flat, thin thing — paper, a book, a card, a document, or (by extension in modern use) a web page. lipu mi could be "my book" or "my document," depending on what's actually flat and holding the words.
Sound or noise in general, and to make one. kalama li mute is "there's a lot of noise."
The sound an animal makes — a moo, woof, meow, or similar — used both to describe such a sound and, playfully, as an interjection imitating one, the way "woof!" can stand alone in English.

Technically, to interact with the official Toki Pona book, as in reading, studying, or using it. Speakers also use pu informally for the book itself, the variety it teaches, or the idea of acting "by the book," but those are extensions of the technical person–book relationship.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "I write this word."
cards.a: mi sitelen e nimi ni.
Air, breath, wind, gas, or an invisible essence/spirit — anything present but unseen. kon li tawa is "there's wind" (air moving); it also covers smell and, more abstractly, spirit or soul.
Cold, or (of food) raw/uncooked — the temperature word, applied to weather, objects, or dishes alike. telo lete is "cold water."
Land, earth, ground, country, or the outdoors in general. ma Kanata is "the land of Canada"; mi lon ma can mean "I'm outside" or "I'm on the ground."
Moon, star, or any celestial body seen in the night sky — Toki Pona doesn't separate "moon" from "star" the way English does. mun li suli is "the moon/a star is big."
Fire, heat, or warmth, and by extension to cook or burn something. telo seli is "hot water"; mi seli e moku is "I cook the food."
Circle, sphere, wheel, or cycle — any round shape or repeating loop, including a year as a cycle of time. sike sin, "new cycle," is one common way to say "new year."
Sun, light, or brightness. suno li lon is "it's daytime/sunny" (literally "the sun is present").
Water, or any liquid. mi moku e telo is "I drink water"; as a modifier, telo marks something as wet or liquid.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "The water is cold."
cards.a: telo li lete.
A land mammal — and, loosely, "animal" in general when the exact kind doesn't matter. soweli covers everything from a mouse to a horse.
Bird, or any flying creature. waso li tawa sewi is "the bird flies upward."
Fish, or any sea creature — whales, octopuses, and dolphins fall under it just as easily as fish do.
Reptile or amphibian — the broad category for lizards, snakes, frogs, and similar creatures that don't fit soweli or waso.
Bug or insect — any small crawling or flying creature in that general size and shape, spiders included even though they're not technically insects.
Plant, herb, leaf, or vegetation in general — the living plant itself, as opposed to something harvested from it. kasi li kule is "the plant is colorful."

Fruit, vegetable, mushroom, or other edible produce. It often refers to something gathered or harvested for food, but it need not be a part of a plant: mushrooms are fungi. mi moku e kili is "I eat fruit, vegetables, or other produce."
Grain, bread, pasta, or any cereal-based food — the specific edible category kili doesn't cover. pan is what a loaf, a bowl of rice, or a plate of noodles all have in common.

cards.q: Translate: "kili ni li pona tawa mi."
cards.a: "I like this fruit, vegetable, mushroom, or other produce" — more literally, "this produce is good to me." Context supplies the specific kind of kili.
Tool, device, or machine — anything built or used to do a job. ilo sitelen would be "a writing/drawing tool," a pen or a computer alike — a single-word modifier needs no pi.
A hard object — stone, rock, or metal. kiwen names the material property (hardness) as much as any specific substance.
A soft or semi-solid substance — paste, powder, dough, mud, clay, or snow. Where kiwen is hard, ko is squishable, and both describe a texture more than one specific material.
Cloth or clothing — fabric in general, and anything made from it worn on the body. len mi is "my clothes."
A long, flexible thing — string, rope, thread, or hair. linja lawa ("head-string") is a common way to say "hair."
A hole, doorway, or window — any opening in a surface. lupa tomo could be a house's door or its window, depending on which opening is meant.
A bump, hill, mountain, or protrusion — and by extension a button, since it physically bumps out. nena suli is "a big hill/mountain."
A long, rigid thing — a stick, rod, or pole. Where linja bends, palisa stays straight and stiff.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "The tool is inside the house."
cards.a: ilo li lon insa tomo.
House, building, or room — any enclosed, indoor structure. tomo moku ("eating house") is one common way to build the idea of "restaurant" out of pieces.
A flat, raised surface meant to be used — a table, chair, bed, shelf, or similar piece of furniture. What unites them is the flat surface something rests or sits on.
Container — box, cup, bag, bowl, or anything that holds something else. poki telo is "water container," a cup or bottle depending on size.
Market, shop, trade, or a business transaction — both the place and the act of exchanging goods. mi tawa esun is "I'm going to the market/store."
Time, a moment, or a period/duration — the general word for anything to do with when or how long. tenpo pini is "past time" (the past); tenpo kama is "coming time" (the future).
Thing, something, or stuff — the most general placeholder noun for an object whose exact nature doesn't matter or isn't known. ijo li lon poki is "there's something in the container."

Way, path, road, method, or system — a route through space or a route through doing something. nasin tawa is literally "a way of going," a road, but also loosely "a way of doing things," a method or custom.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "The thing is at the market."
cards.a: ijo li lon esun.
To work, make, do, or act — and, as a noun, work or a job. mi pali e tomo is "I make/build a house"; mi pali alone is simply "I work" or "I'm doing something."
To give, put, send, release, or produce — moving something from one place, person, or state to another. mi pana e ni tawa sina is "I give this to you."
To have, hold, or contain — possession or physical containment, treated as the same idea. mi jo e ilo is "I have a tool."
To eat or drink, and, as a noun, food in general — Toki Pona doesn't separate eating from drinking the way English does. moku pona is "good food."

To hunt, forage, gather, or try to get something — the effort of pursuing and obtaining, whether that's an animal, food, or an opportunity. mi alasa e kili is "I gather fruit." Many modern speakers also use alasa as the preverb "try to."
To fight, and, as a noun, a fight, conflict, battle, or competition — any struggle between opposing sides, physical or otherwise. utala li lon is "there's a fight/conflict happening."
Sex, or to have sex — the plain, clinical word for sexual or intimate activity, used the same matter-of-fact way any other action word is used.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "I give the tool to you."
cards.a: mi pana e ilo tawa sina.
To open, start, or begin — both a physical opening and the start of an event or action. mi open e tomo is "I open the house/building." As a preverb, mi open pali is "I start working."
To end, finish, or close, and by extension "past" as a description of time. As a preverb, mi pini pali is "I stop/finish working"; tenpo pini is "the past."

To come, arrive, or become — both physical arrival and a change of state. mi kama tawa tomo is "I arrive home." As a preverb, ona li kama pona is "they become well/good" — the root of kama pona, "welcome," literally "become good [here]."
To stay, wait, remain, or keep/protect something in place. mi awen lon tomo is "I stay at home"; o awen! is "wait!" As a preverb, mi awen pali is "I continue working."
Away, absent, or gone, and, as a verb with e, to remove something. ona li weka is "they're away/gone"; mi weka e ijo is "I remove the thing."
To break, mess up, or cause an accident — and, as a noun or interjection, damage, a mistake, or a mild "oops!"/curse. ilo li pakala is "the tool is broken."
To die, or dead/death — and, taking e, to kill. soweli li moli is "the animal died/is dead"; mi moli e soweli is "I kill the animal."
To sleep or rest, and, as a noun, sleep itself. mi lape is "I sleep/I'm sleeping" or "I'm resting."

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "I open the container."
cards.a: mi open e poki.
Good, simple, nice, or well — Toki Pona's single most-used word, and, as a verb with e, "to fix" or "to improve." o pona e ni is "please fix this."
Bad, negative, excessive, or unpleasant — the natural opposite of pona, covering everything from "not great" to "genuinely harmful" depending on context and tone.
Big, large, tall, or important — size and significance share the same word, the way English sometimes says "a big deal."
Small, little, or young — the opposite of suli in both senses, covering physical smallness and being minor/young.
New, fresh, additional, or another — something just arrived or added. tenpo sin, "new time," is one way to say "a new era" or mark a fresh start.
Different, other, or changed — and, as a verb, "to change." ni li ante is "this is different"; mi ante e ni is "I change this."

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "This tool is small."
cards.a: ilo ni li lili.
Strong, powerful, or energetic — and, as a noun, strength, energy, or power itself. jan wawa is "a strong/powerful person."
Unusual, strange, odd, unexpected, silly, or intoxicated. ni li nasa can mean "this is unusual"; telo nasa can be an intoxicating drink. Context supplies the intended sense.
Dirty, gross, unsanitary, or taboo — anything that provokes disgust or is considered off-limits. telo jaki is "dirty water."
Sweet, or cute/adorable — both the taste and the charm sense, the same overlap English sometimes makes ("sweet" as in candy or as in kind).
Up, above, high, or elevated — and, by extension, sacred or divine, the way "the heavens above" carries both a direction and a reverence. mun li lon sewi is "the moon is up above."
Down, below, or low — the opposite of sewi — and, by extension, humble or subordinate. As a verb it can mean "to defeat" or "to lower/humiliate."
Spice, seasoning, or garnish — and more generally, something extra or additional layered onto a base. moku namako is "spiced/seasoned food."

cards.q: Give one possible Toki Pona sentence for "The person drinks an intoxicating drink."
cards.a: jan li moku e telo nasa. Here nasa describes the drink. Without an alcohol-related context, telo nasa could instead mean any strange or unusual liquid.

Color, or colorful/multicolored in general — the umbrella word before any specific hue is named. In some modern community usage, kule is also used figuratively for queer identity; this sense is not universal, and many speakers use the word only for color.
Red.
Yellow — and, loosely, colors in the yellow-to-orange-to-brown range that don't have their own dedicated word.
Blue — and, since Toki Pona doesn't have a separate word for green, also green and blue-green. Which shade is meant comes from context or from adding a modifier.
White, pale, or light-colored — covering not just white itself but light shades in general, the way pimeja covers dark ones.
Black, dark, or dark-colored — the counterpart to walo, covering darkness and dark shades broadly rather than only literal black.

cards.q: Translate into Toki Pona: "This house is red."
cards.a: tomo ni li loje.

An interjection expressing emphasis, emotion, or confirmation — like "ah," "oh," "wow," "ha," or an acknowledging "yes/indeed." It can stand alone or color another phrase: pona a! is "good, wow!" or "great!"
Money, currency, or wealth — and, in some contexts, valuable livestock, echoing how many real languages' words for money trace back to cattle as an early store of value.

cards.q: This course has covered roughly 120 core words. Is that the entire language?
cards.a: It is a widely shared foundation, commonly called nimi pu because the words are documented in the 2014 book Toki Pona: The Language of Good. That book presented kin, namako, and oko as synonyms of a, sin, and lukin; many speakers now distinguish them. The 2021 Toki Pona Dictionary (ku) recorded community usage rather than declaring a new mandatory vocabulary; nimi ku suli is a community label for 17 words that received especially broad use, such as soko for mushroom and tonsi for nonbinary or gender-diverse people. These words add convenient conventions, not concepts that were impossible to express before: for example, lukin already means "eye," while oko is another word some speakers use for it. Speakers vary in which words they use, and the language has no permanently closed master list.

cards.q: How could you describe a mushroom without using "soko"?
cards.a: One concise option is kili ma, "earth/ground produce." You could add more detail for the situation; Toki Pona usually describes the relevant qualities instead of requiring one fixed word for every species or object.
